newsitem.title: USA: Palm Beach Cty, Fla., bonds linked to bankruptcy.
newsitem.headline: Palm Beach Cty, Fla., bonds linked to bankruptcy.

text.p: Municipal bond traders in Florida said they had seen no immediate impact on three series of Palm Beach County industrial development bonds linked to biomass cogeneration partnerships that filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection Wednesday.
The plants were financed in part with the county's Solid Waste Industrial Development Revenue Bonds, in the following series:
--Okeelanta Power Limited Partnership Project, Series 1993A, with an aggregate principal amount of $160 million.
--Osceola Power Limited Partnership Project, tax-exempt Series 1994A, issued in an aggregate principal amount of $120.5 million.
--Osceola Power Limited Partnership Project, taxable Series 1994 B, issued in an aggregate principal amount of $8,000,000.
One Florida trader of high-yield munis said he had not seen any of the bonds offered for several months, but that they had previously traded at "a pretty deep discount."
"It's been pretty common knowledge in the street that they've been in trouble," he said.
Bob Lind, high-yield muni trader for Raymond James & Associates, also said he had seen no recent trading but that there had been a small burst of sales six or seven months ago.
"It's fairly illiquid, so any activity was greater than normal," Lind said.
Assistant Palm Beach County Attorney Paul King said the bonds were strictly a conduit issue and are not backed by any pledge of county revenues.

"As far as I know we don't have any reason at this point to assert any kind of claim," King said. "Obviously we don't want the bonds to go into default, but the organization that filed for Chapter 11 is still operating."

The partnerships that sought bankruptcy protection are owned by owned by Pacific Gas & Electric Co, a unit of PG&E Corp and Bechtel. They said the bankruptcy filing was necessary because of a legal dispute with Florida Power & Light Co over FPL's obligation to buy power produced by the two biomass plants in Okeelanta and Osceola, Fla.
FPL first raised the issue in a lawsuit in early January, which could account for the previous burst of trading Lind described.
Chapter 11 bankruptcy allows companies to continue operating while reorganizing their debt.
